title: Spatial-Mode Selection for Local Mineral Absorption Spectroscopy
authors: Qipeng Qian, Jialiang Jin, Shihao Wang, Yuntao Qian
abstract: Absorption-band depth measures the fractional decrease in mineral reflectance below its local continuum. Recovering this feature strength for a small mineral region supports quantitative comparisons between regions, but diffraction mixes its light with the surroundings. Conventional spectral fitting can separate mean contributions; it cannot remove background photon noise already recorded. We develop a quantum-inspired measurement framework that uses spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) to retain the target absorption response while reducing background acceptance before detection. The framework connects finite mineral-region geometry and reference spectra to estimation precision. A loss-dependent design condition identifies when adding SPADE exposure improves on direct imaging (DI) under fixed-response Poisson measurements with unknown scene parameters. Joint inference from initial DI observations and both mode ports estimates target depth together with an unknown, spatially shared background spectrum. In equal-time simulations that include localization uncertainty, alignment time, calibration, and detector costs, this acquisition reduces depth root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 14\%--26\% across five absorption strengths relative to all-pixel DI with the same background freedom. These results use a supplied target feature shape and geometry, with target continuum slope fitted and curvature fixed. The analysis separates optical selectivity from parameter ambiguity and acquisition cost, providing a quantitative basis for spatial-mode receiver design in local mineral spectroscopy.
summary: This paper introduces a quantum-inspired measurement technique called Spatial-Mode Demultiplexing (SPADE) to improve the measurement of mineral absorption depth. By splitting the light into two orthogonal spatial modes, the method effectively suppresses background photon noise that plagues conventional spectral analysis. This results in a significant reduction in the estimation error for local mineral spectroscopy.
main_problem: The core problem is quantitatively measuring the absorption depth of a small mineral region while accurately separating this target signal from background photon noise introduced by diffraction and the surrounding environment.
main_result: The proposed quantum-inspired acquisition method reduces the depth root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 14%–26% compared to direct imaging (DI) under equivalent background freedom.
method: The authors developed a framework using Spatial-Mode Demultiplexing (SPADE), which separates the optical field into a selected mode and its orthogonal complement to suppress background noise before detection.
model_or_system: The system is local mineral absorption spectroscopy, involving a finite mineral target embedded in a background. The model incorporates concepts from diffraction, spectral fitting, and quantum-inspired measurement theory.
key_observables: Target absorption depth (fractional decrease in reflectance), unknown spatially shared background spectrum, and the root-mean-square error (RMSE) of the depth estimate.
important_parameters: Absorption strength, background photon noise, spatial mode selection efficiency, and acquisition time/cost.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes fixed-response Poisson measurements, and the initial modeling relies on supplied target feature shapes and geometries.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows how Binary SPADE separates the optical field into two modes to reduce background noise. Figure 2 illustrates the experimental setup, showing a finite target in a background and the sequence of DI and adaptive SPADE measurements.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the spectral measurement challenge to introducing the SPADE framework, detailing the joint inference process using initial DI data and dual-port SPADE measurements, and concluding with quantitative performance comparisons against DI.
why_interesting: The use of spatial-mode demultiplexing to suppress background noise in a spectral measurement is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems, as it models noise reduction techniques analogous to quantum measurement strategies.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Binary SPADE separates a selected optical field mode from its orthogonal complement and records a spectrum at each port. A mode matching the field from a point near the target can retain much of a small target’s light while directing much of an extended background to the other port. Both spectra remain target/background mixtures and are fitted jointly for depth. DI records pixel spectra instead. The schematic illustrates the principle; precision depends on scene geometry, spectra, and receiver loss.

Fig. 2. C4 scene and acquisition. (a) Finite calcite target in dolomite with a left-to-right brightness gradient, before diffraction. The blue cross is the fixed-comparison mode center; the inset shows its offset from the target. Coordinates use L = 1.09975 mm [(6)]. (b) USGS component reflectances before mixing/filtering. Target depth is the fractional dip below the orange dashed continuum at maximum absorption. (c) Preparation supplies target shape and geometry. DI observes for 9.5 s; adaptive acquisition uses 1.8 s DI localization, 0.2 s alignment, and 7.0 s dual-port observation, fitted jointly. Dark and calibration complete the 10 s budgets (Table III).

Fig. 3. Ideal C4 comparison at 2335.97 nm, with L = 1.09975 mm. (a) Target retention versus background acceptance for circular DI regions at pitches 0.25L and 0.125L. The marked region maximizes summed-count Fisher information. (b) Information for equal 1 s exposures: the best summed region, all DI pixels/optimal local weights, and both mode ports. The mode center is (0.5L, 0) and target center (0.62L, 0.08L). Brightness, position, and background are known; extra transmission is unity and crosstalk zero. SPADE exceeds even the finer-DI information.

Fig. 4. Fixed-response design with an estimated C4 background. (a) Effective depth information relative to DI versus mode exposure fraction. Solid curves use the nominal center at labeled transmissions; the blue dashed curve uses the true center at transmission 0.70. The horizontal line denotes equal information. (b) Information in 1 s for DI and 20/80 DI–mode acquisition, retaining one or both ports. Background level/shape are fixed in the known group; all 25 values are fitted in the estimated group. The complement primarily constrains background. Both panels include 12 nm response and known 1% crosstalk, with unknown target brightness, slope, and position. Responses/calibration are fixed;...

Fig. 5. Complete 10 s acquisitions with the same freely estimated background in both receivers, 400 trials per arm. (a) Depth RMSE at five true depths with fixed target continuum/profile; lines guide the eye. (b) Adaptive/DI ratios with pointwise 95% intervals (dark) and seven-comparison Bonferroni intervals (light); values below one favor adaptive acquisition. Reference-error tests use new perturbations of one standard error of the mean (SEM), with 12 nm correlation; the last also applies a shared offset within ±0.5 nm. Adaptive trials include DI localization, alignment time, calibration, and detector costs.
